n: Job continues his discourse. With no further reply from Zophar, Job now delivers his closing statements (chapters 27–31).

f.g: Hebrew mashal — a formal discourse or poem, not just a short story.

n: Job swears an oath by the living God — the same God he feels has denied him justice and made his life bitter.

f.g: A solemn oath formula, like “as surely as God lives.”

n: As long as he has breath — the breath God himself gave — Job makes his promise.

f.w: the spirit of God is in my nostrils

n: He will never speak wickedness or lies. In other words, he will not falsely confess sins he didn’t commit just to please his friends.
Job will never agree that his friends are right. Until he dies he will not let go of his integrity.

f.g: Wholeness, blamelessness — the very quality God praised in Job.

n: He holds tightly to his righteousness, and his conscience does not condemn him for any day of his life.

f.w: my heart shall not reproach me

n: Job wishes that his accusers be treated like the wicked — they deserve the fate they assign to him.

f.w: Let mine enemy be as the wicked
f.g: A legal-style curse on false accusers.

n: What hope does a godless person have when God takes his life, no matter how much he gained?
Will God hear his cry when trouble comes? By contrast, Job still cries to God.
Can the godless delight in God or keep calling on him? Job can, and does — which shows he is no hypocrite.
Job promises to teach his friends about God’s ways and hold nothing back.
They have all seen these things themselves — so why speak such nonsense?
Verses 13–23 describe the fate of the wicked. Job may be quoting or agreeing with the friends that God will ultimately punish evil, even if not on their timetable.

f.w: This is the portion of a wicked man

n: Many children may be born to him, but they fall by the sword or go hungry.

f.w: multiplied, it is for the sword

n: His survivors die by plague, and even his widows don’t mourn him.

f.g: “Death” here may mean plague or pestilence.

n: He may pile up silver like dust and clothes like heaps of clay…

f.g: Clothing — a form of wealth in the ancient world.

n: …but the righteous will wear the clothes and the innocent will share the silver.

f.w: the just shall put it on

n: His house is as flimsy as a moth’s cocoon or a watchman’s temporary shelter in a field.

f.g: A temporary hut built by a field guard during harvest.

n: He goes to bed rich, but one morning he opens his eyes and everything is gone.

f.g: Probably “he will not do so again” — his wealth will vanish.

n: Terrors sweep over him like floodwaters, and a storm snatches him in the night.
The scorching east wind lifts him and sweeps him away.
It hurls itself against him without mercy as he tries desperately to flee.
People clap their hands in scorn and hiss him from his place — signs of contempt and relief at his fall.
